magnetic-materials-001.question: Which type of magnetism does a material show if its magnetic susceptibility χ is negative and very small, on the order of 10⁻⁵?
magnetic-materials-001.explanation: Diamagnetism is the property in which an applied magnetic field changes the orbital motion of electrons and produces a weak magnetization opposite to the field; χ is negative, with a magnitude of about 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁵. All materials have it, but in copper, water and most organic substances, which have no unpaired electrons, it is the only magnetism that appears. Paramagnetism is the slight alignment of randomly oriented atomic moments along the field, and χ is positive. Antiferromagnetism is an ordering of neighboring moments antiparallel to one another, and χ is again small and positive. The negative sign of χ is what identifies diamagnetism, and superconductors show perfect diamagnetism with χ = −1.

magnetic-materials-002.question: Which statement correctly describes the ferrimagnetism shown by ferrites such as magnetite (Fe₃O₄)?
choices: All atomic moments are aligned parallel, so it is essentially the same as ferromagnetism
The moments of two sublattices are aligned antiparallel and are equal in size, so the net spontaneous magnetization is zero
The moments of two sublattices are aligned antiparallel but differ in size, so they do not cancel and a spontaneous magnetization remains
magnetic-materials-002.explanation: In a ferrimagnet, the magnetic moments on two kinds of sites in the crystal (sublattices) are aligned antiparallel to each other by the exchange interaction. Because the moments on the two sublattices differ in size or number, they do not cancel completely, and a spontaneous magnetization equal to the difference remains. Macroscopically a ferrimagnet shows domains and hysteresis just as a ferromagnet does, but its saturation magnetization is smaller than that of ferromagnetic metals such as iron. Parallel alignment of all moments is ferromagnetism, and antiparallel moments of equal size that cancel is antiferromagnetism. Ferrites are oxides with a high electrical resistivity, so eddy currents hardly flow in them, and they are used as cores at high frequencies.

magnetic-materials-003.question: Take the magnetic moment per atom of iron (BCC, lattice parameter 0.2866 nm) as 2.22 µB. Which value is closest to the saturation magnetization Ms at 0 K, when all the moments are aligned? Take the Bohr magneton as µB = 9.27×10⁻²⁴ A·m².
magnetic-materials-003.explanation: A BCC unit cell contains 2 atoms, so the number density of atoms is n = 2/a³ = 2/(0.2866×10⁻⁹ m)³ ≈ 8.50×10²⁸ m⁻³. The saturation magnetization is the magnetic moment per unit volume, so Ms = n × 2.22 µB = 8.50×10²⁸ × 2.22 × 9.27×10⁻²⁴ ≈ 1.7×10⁶ A/m. Expressed as µ₀Ms this is about 2.2 T, in good agreement with the saturation flux density of iron. About 8.7×10⁵ A/m counts the unit cell as containing 1 atom, and about 3.5×10⁶ A/m counts 4 atoms as in FCC. The moment per atom is not a whole number because the 3d electrons responsible for magnetism form a band.

magnetic-materials-004.question: Magnetite Fe₃O₄ has the inverse spinel structure: the A sites (tetrahedral) hold one Fe³⁺, the B sites (octahedral) hold one Fe³⁺ and one Fe²⁺, and the moments on the A and B sites are antiparallel. Taking Fe³⁺ as 5 µB and Fe²⁺ as 4 µB, with only spin contributing, what is the magnetic moment per Fe₃O₄ formula unit?
magnetic-materials-004.explanation: The B-site moment is 5 + 4 = 9 µB and the A-site moment is 5 µB, and since they are antiparallel, 9 − 5 = 4 µB remains. You can also think of the Fe³⁺ ions on the A and B sites as exactly canceling each other, leaving only the contribution of Fe²⁺. The value obtained from the measured saturation magnetization is about 4.1 µB, in good agreement with this estimate. 14 µB assumes all the moments are parallel (the mistake of treating it as ferromagnetic), and 0 µB assumes everything cancels (the mistake of treating it as antiferromagnetic). Replacing Fe²⁺ with another divalent ion (such as Ni²⁺ or Mn²⁺) changes the saturation magnetization according to that ion's moment.

magnetic-materials-005.question: What is the main reason a ferromagnet splits into many magnetic domains even without an external field?
choices: To lower the energy of the exchange interaction, which tends to align the moments of neighboring atoms parallel
To lower the magnetostatic (demagnetizing-field) energy of the poles that appear on the surface when the whole body is uniformly magnetized
Because even below the Curie temperature, thermal vibration randomizes the directions of the atomic magnetic moments
magnetic-materials-005.explanation: If the whole crystal is magnetized in one direction, large magnetic poles appear on its surface, creating fields outside and inside (the demagnetizing field inside), with a large magnetostatic energy. Splitting into domains with different directions lets the poles cancel and lowers this energy greatly. On the other hand, inside a domain wall at the boundary between domains the moments turn gradually, so the energy rises by the exchange and anisotropy energies. The actual domain size is set by the balance between the two. The exchange interaction acts to align all the moments, so splitting into domains actually increases the exchange energy. Moments randomized by thermal vibration describe the paramagnetic state above the Curie temperature.

magnetic-materials-006.question: As particles of a ferromagnet are made smaller, from a few µm down to nm sizes, which statement correctly describes how their coercivity changes?
choices: Coercivity is a material constant set only by the magnetocrystalline anisotropy, so it stays almost constant regardless of size
Smaller particles have fewer domain walls and reverse less easily, so it keeps increasing monotonically down to the nm scale
It peaks near the critical single-domain size, then falls toward zero as the particles become superparamagnetic
magnetic-materials-006.explanation: Large particles contain many domains, and their magnetization reverses by the motion of domain walls, which move even in weak fields, so the coercivity is small. Making the particles smaller reduces the number of walls, and below a critical size they become single-domain particles with no walls. Reversing the magnetization of a single-domain particle requires rotating the whole magnetization against the magnetic anisotropy, so the coercivity peaks around this size. Making them smaller still makes the energy barrier to reversal, KV, small compared with the thermal energy, so the magnetization reverses spontaneously by thermal activation (superparamagnetism) and the coercivity approaches zero. Coercivity depends strongly on particle size and microstructure, not only on the anisotropy, so it is not constant, and below the critical size it does not keep increasing. Particles for magnetic recording media are designed between these upper and lower limits.

magnetic-materials-007.question: Take the energy barrier for thermal reversal of the magnetization of a single-domain particle of volume V as KV (K is the magnetic anisotropy constant); for a measurement time of about 100 s, KV = 25kT is a guide to the boundary for superparamagnetism. With K = 1.1×10⁴ J/m³, a temperature of 300 K and the Boltzmann constant k = 1.38×10⁻²³ J/K, which value is closest to the upper limit of the diameter of a spherical particle that becomes superparamagnetic?
magnetic-materials-007.explanation: The boundary volume is V = 25kT/K = 25 × 1.38×10⁻²³ × 300/(1.1×10⁴) ≈ 9.4×10⁻²⁴ m³. From the volume of a sphere V = πd³/6, d = (6V/π)^(1/3) ≈ 2.6×10⁻⁸ m, so particles with diameters of about 26 nm or less become superparamagnetic. About 13 nm mistakes the calculated diameter for the radius, and about 9 nm drops the factor of 25 and uses KV = kT. The factor of 25 comes from ln(100 s/10⁻⁹ s) ≈ 25, taking the attempt time for reversal as about 10⁻⁹ s. The diameter is inversely proportional to the cube root of K, so materials with larger anisotropy can keep their magnetization stable even in smaller particles.

magnetic-materials-008.question: What is the main reason permalloy, Fe with about 78% Ni, shows an extremely high permeability?
choices: Adding Ni roughly doubles the saturation magnetization relative to pure iron, giving a large flux density even in a weak field
Its magnetocrystalline anisotropy and magnetostriction are both nearly zero, so domain walls move and magnetization rotates easily
Rapid quenching refines its grains to nanometer sizes, so that the magnetocrystalline anisotropy averages out and cancels
magnetic-materials-008.explanation: A high permeability requires the magnetization to change greatly in a weak field. Magnetization rotation is hindered by magnetocrystalline anisotropy, and if there is magnetostriction, the magnetoelastic energy coupled to internal stresses hinders domain-wall motion. In the Fe–Ni system, at compositions around 80% Ni both the magnetocrystalline anisotropy constant and the magnetostriction constant approach zero, and heat treatment that adjusts the degree of ordering can make the anisotropy even smaller, so a very high permeability is obtained. The saturation flux density of permalloy is considerably lower than that of pure iron (about 2.2 T), so the option citing a saturation magnetization larger than that of pure iron is wrong. Making grains nanometer-sized so that the anisotropy averages out is the idea behind nanocrystalline soft magnetic alloys, not the reason for permalloy.

magnetic-materials-009.question: Grain-oriented electrical steel (Fe with about 3% Si) used for transformer cores has especially low loss and high permeability when magnetized along the rolling direction. Which reason is correct?
choices: The grains are aligned in the Goss orientation {110}<001>, so the easy axis <100> points along the rolling direction
The texture is controlled so that <111>, the easy axis of iron, is aligned with the rolling direction
The grains are refined and randomly oriented so that the sheet magnetizes equally easily in every direction
magnetic-materials-009.explanation: Iron is cubic, and because of magnetocrystalline anisotropy the <100> directions are the easiest to magnetize (easy axes) and the <111> directions the hardest. Grain-oriented electrical steel is given coarse grains in the Goss orientation, with {110} planes parallel to the sheet surface and <001> along the rolling direction, by secondary recrystallization using inhibitors (fine MnS or AlN precipitates). Magnetized along the rolling direction, it therefore approaches saturation in a weak field and its loss is small. The option treating <111> as the easy axis confuses the easy and hard axes. Non-oriented electrical steel, with random orientations, is used for motor cores, where the direction of the flux rotates. Si is added to raise the electrical resistivity and reduce eddy-current loss.

magnetic-materials-010.question: Assume the eddy-current loss of electrical steel sheet is proportional to t²f²Bm², where t is the sheet thickness, f the frequency and Bm the peak flux density (with the same resistivity). At the same frequency and flux density, by roughly what factor does the eddy-current loss change if the thickness is reduced from 0.50 mm to 0.35 mm?
magnetic-materials-010.explanation: The eddy-current loss is proportional to the square of the thickness, so (0.35/0.50)² = 0.70² = 0.49, about 0.49 times the original, or roughly half. About 0.70 times assumes it is proportional to the thickness, and about 0.34 times assumes it is proportional to the cube. In a thinner sheet the emf induced across its cross section by the changing flux is smaller and the current paths are narrower, so the loss falls as the square of the thickness. That is why cores are built by stacking thin sheets with insulated surfaces. Hysteresis loss, however, hardly depends on thickness, so the total core loss does not fall all the way to half. Adding Si to raise the resistivity is another way to suppress eddy currents.

magnetic-materials-011.question: An alternating field at 50 Hz is applied to electrical steel sheet with an electrical resistivity of 4.8×10⁻⁷ Ω·m and a relative permeability of 5000. Which value is closest to the skin depth δ = √(2ρ/(ωµ))? Take ω = 2πf, µ = µᵣµ₀ and µ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m.
magnetic-materials-011.explanation: ωµ = 2π × 50 × 5000 × 4π×10⁻⁷ ≈ 1.97, so 2ρ/(ωµ) = 9.6×10⁻⁷/1.97 ≈ 4.9×10⁻⁷ m², and δ ≈ 7.0×10⁻⁴ m = 0.70 mm. About 0.49 mm drops the 2 in the formula, and about 1.7 mm substitutes the frequency f directly in place of ω. The skin depth is a measure of how deep alternating flux can penetrate into the sheet; unless the sheet is well thinner than this, the flux does not reach its center and the material is not used effectively. Electrical steel about 0.35 mm thick satisfies this condition at 50 Hz, but δ shrinks in inverse proportion to the square root of frequency, so at kHz and above, thin ribbons of amorphous alloys or high-resistivity ferrites are used.

magnetic-materials-012.question: On the demagnetization curve of a permanent magnet, let the magnitude of the reverse field that brings the flux density B to zero be the coercivity HcB, and the magnitude of the reverse field that brings the magnetization M to zero be the intrinsic coercivity HcJ. From the relation B = µ₀(H + M), which relationship between them is correct?
choices: Always HcJ = HcB, regardless of the material
magnetic-materials-012.explanation: When B reaches zero at a reverse field H = −HcB, B = µ₀(H + M) gives M = HcB > 0, so the magnetization is still positive. Bringing M to zero requires an even stronger reverse field, so HcJ ≥ HcB. The options HcJ ≤ HcB and always equal are therefore wrong. Also, in a reverse field M does not exceed the remanent magnetization, so HcB cannot exceed Br/µ₀. In materials with a very large HcJ, such as neodymium magnets, HcB levels off near this upper limit of Br/µ₀. Whether a magnet resists demagnetization at high temperature or in a strong reverse field is judged by HcJ, which shows whether the magnetization itself reverses. In soft magnetic materials with small coercivities, the difference between the two is negligibly small.

magnetic-materials-013.question: For an ideal permanent magnet whose demagnetization curve is the straight line B = Br + µ₀H (with a sufficiently large HcJ) and whose remanent flux density is Br = 1.40 T, which value is closest to the maximum energy product (BH)max? Take µ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m.
magnetic-materials-013.explanation: On the straight line in the second quadrant, the magnitude of the product of B and H, |BH| = (Br + µ₀H)(−H), is greatest at H = −Br/(2µ₀), B = Br/2, giving (BH)max = Br²/(4µ₀). Substituting values, 1.40²/(4 × 4π×10⁻⁷) = 1.96/(5.03×10⁻⁶) ≈ 3.9×10⁵ J/m³, about 390 kJ/m³ (about 49 MGOe). About 1560 kJ/m³ multiplies the two ends of the line, Br and Br/µ₀, and about 780 kJ/m³ divides by 2 only once. The theoretical upper limit estimated by the same formula from the saturation magnetization of Nd₂Fe₁₄B (about 1.6 T) is about 510 kJ/m³, and high-performance commercial neodymium magnets reach about 80% of it (about 400 to 440 kJ/m³).

magnetic-materials-014.question: What is the main material reason that neodymium magnets, with Nd₂Fe₁₄B as the main phase, can have a large coercivity?
choices: It is cubic with almost no magnetocrystalline anisotropy, so the magnetization is stable in any direction
Its saturation magnetization is as large as about 1.6 T, and a larger saturation magnetization always means a larger coercivity
It is tetragonal, with a strong uniaxial magnetocrystalline anisotropy along the c axis
magnetic-materials-014.explanation: A guide to the upper limit of coercivity is the anisotropy field HA = 2K/(µ₀Ms); the larger K is, the harder it is to turn the magnetization away from the easy axis. Nd₂Fe₁₄B is tetragonal and, owing to the contribution of the Nd 4f electrons, has a strong uniaxial magnetocrystalline anisotropy along the c axis, with µ₀HA reaching about 7.5 T. The actual coercivity is much smaller than HA because reversed domains nucleate at places such as grain surfaces, and it is raised by controlling the microstructure, such as the grain-boundary phase. A cubic crystal with almost no anisotropy is the condition for soft magnetic materials such as permalloy. The saturation magnetization of Nd₂Fe₁₄B, about 1.6 T, is large and raises the remanent flux density, but Ms is in the denominator of the formula for HA, so the coercivity does not necessarily increase.

magnetic-materials-015.question: What is the main purpose of adding Dy or Tb to neodymium magnets used at high temperatures, such as in electric-vehicle motors?
choices: To raise the remanent flux density and thus the maximum energy product
To raise the Curie temperature above 1000°C and prevent thermal demagnetization
To compensate for the coercivity that falls as the temperature rises, by raising the anisotropy field
magnetic-materials-015.explanation: Nd₂Fe₁₄B has a rather low Curie temperature of about 310°C, and as the temperature rises its magnetocrystalline anisotropy falls and its coercivity drops sharply. To prevent demagnetization at the motor's operating temperature, part of the Nd is replaced by Dy or Tb to raise the anisotropy field and the coercivity. However, the magnetic moments of Dy and Tb couple antiparallel to those of Fe, so the more is added, the lower the saturation magnetization, and the remanent flux density and maximum energy product actually decrease. The Curie temperature also stays at a few hundred °C with this addition and does not exceed 1000°C. Because Dy and Tb are expensive and their resources are unevenly distributed, methods that diffuse them only into the grain surfaces to reduce the amount used have been put into practice.
